name: Evaluating mechanisms underlying disturbance-related demographic change
description: Human development is expanding rapidly into wildlands to keep up with exponential population growth, forcing wildlife to either emigrate or adapt to increased disturbance. Species that adapt often exhibit behavioral changes that can have subsequent survival consequences. Despite a strong focus on urbanization?s impact on species behavior, there is increasing evidence of behavioral shifts occurring at a low-density, rural scale. In particular, changes in antipredator behavior and sociality may be altered by small-scale anthropogenic development. Antipredator vigilance and flight initiation distance can directly affect survival-related behaviors such as foraging or reproduction. Social structure and individual social relationships have been found to have complex impacts on species survival. While both vigilance and sociality have been studied extensively, little is known about how built structures may alter these behaviors by impeding an animal?s visibility of a landscape. The yellow-bellied marmot (Marmota flaviventer), a social, behaviorally adaptable rodent, is an ideal model species to analyze the relationship between rural human disturbance and behavior. Previous studies have determined that marmot behaviors, such as vigilance and mating, influence their survival, which may impact their demography. Marmots can acclimate to humans, which may also have long-term survival consequences. My study goals are to: 1) determine whether there are significant differences in antipredator behaviors in disturbed versus undisturbed areas; 2) determine whether there are significant differences in social behaviors in disturbed versus undisturbed areas; and 3) use statistical models to pinpoint any underlying mechanisms that may influence species demography in response to human disturbance. I aim to fill a crucial knowledge gap in how wildlife are influenced by rural anthropogenic development through changes in landscape visibility. My results can be useful for future studies on how disturbance influences wildlife behavior and may create novel insights for the conservation management of social species in human-modified environments.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Long-term research

name: Interactive effects of biotic and abiotic conditions on local adaptation
description:
Climate change is imposing novel selection, disrupting local adaptation, shifting geographic distributions, and altering species composition and diversity of ecological communities. Accordingly, climate change acts directly on species through new abiotic conditions, as well as indirectly through altered biotic interactions. Here, we seek to test mechanistic hypotheses about evolution in complex environments where correlated suites of traits evolve in response to abiotic and biotic agents of selection. Specifically, we propose to examine the mechanistic basis of local adaptation to current abiotic and biotic conditions in the emerging ecological model plant, Boechera stricta (Brassicaceae), in the Colorado Rocky Mountains. We focus on plant-herbivore interactions, as they provide exceptional opportunities for dissecting the direct and indirect effects of climate change. We will then predict plant evolutionary responses to projected future abiotic and biotic environments. _x000D_
To evaluate how abiotic conditions and the biotic community have interacted to shape local adaptation and exert selection on functional traits (Aim 1), we will first conduct a multifactorial manipulation of herbivory, snow dynamics, and water availability in three field gardens at different elevations. We will then characterize herbivore communities across elevational gradients to project future distributions and abundances (Aim 2). Finally, based on these projections, we will investigate how adaptive landscapes will shift under climate change by exposing B. stricta transplants to current and future abiotic conditions and herbivore levels in high and low elevation gardens (Aim 3 and 4). We hypothesize that climate change favors novel suites of traits, such as the rapid development of high elevation families combined with the drought tolerance and herbivore resistance of low elevation families. Further, to test the hypothesis that genetic trade-offs restrict adaptation, we will contrast natural accessions with existing genetic constraints vs. recombinant inbred lines that allow an unconstrained response to selection. Finally, we will examine the genetic basis of local adaptation by mapping quantitative trait loci and test whether the fitness of local alleles declines under climate change. _x000D_
	 _x000D_
Despite extensive work characterizing local adaptation, we still know little about the processes through which species adapt to the simultaneous, likely interactive, effects of multiple abiotic and biotic agents of selection. Dissecting the contributions of climatic and biotic factors to local adaptation and selection will enable us to forecast how climate change could alter adaptive evolution and influence the risk of extinction. The proposed studies will reveal the extent to which climate change could favor novel suites of traits, whether genetic constraints could restrict adaptation, and whether climate change could increase the vulnerability of local populations to decline. Collectively, our field experiments will identify the functional traits and genetic basis of local adaptation to complex environments and evaluate the evolutionary and ecological consequences of projected future, novel environments.
researchAreas: Climate change; Genetics; Phenology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

name: Intra-annual variation in pollen and nectar nutrition
description: I present a project to (1) assess intra-seasonal variation in the quantity and nutritional content of pollen and nectar and (2) link nutritional variation to foraging patterns in a community of wild insect pollinators. It is reasonable to expect that nutritional traits may exhibit substantive intra-seasonal variation, likely in response to phenological and environmental drivers, but we currently lack any framework for assessing the extent of such variation and how it could impact survival, foraging, and pollen transfer by insect pollinators. My goal with this project is to characterize weekly variation in nectar and pollen nutrients and assess how that variation impacts pollinator foraging and pollen collection. I hypothesize that the nutritional traits of pollen and nectar will vary in response to phenological and environmental drivers and that this intra-seasonal nutritional variation has a substantive impact on pollinator foraging.

name: Forecasting integrated plant-aphid dynamics in a rapidly warming community
description: Changing weather patterns are expected to disrupt the lifecycles and population growth of many organisms, especially ones that are sensitive to changes in temperature like insects. But when insects rely on other organisms like plants, microbes or other insects for food, protection or habitat, it becomes harder to predict how they will respond, because these organisms may also be affected by these changes. Because mountain ecosystems are harsher environments, not as many different species live there, making it easier to observe these interactions. This project will use many years of observations of aphids, ants, plants and microbes to build a computer model that will integrate these interactions and make predictions about how different patterns of environmental change will affect the abundance and long-term survival of these species.

name: Local adaptation in plant-aphid dynamics across a temperature gradient
description: Insect herbivores such as aphids play an outsized role in both natural and agricultural ecosystems. Consequently, understanding factors that control aphid abundance is critical for ecosystem management. Temperature can directly impact aphid development, growth, and survival and shift how these insect herbivores interact with plants. Genetic differences among aphid and plant populations can also influence how these organisms respond to rising temperatures. This project will assess local adaptation in plant-aphid interactions across a temperature gradient in a well-studied Rocky Mountain ecosystem. Findings from this work will be used to create models that predict plant-aphid dynamics under different climate conditions, develop educational materials for K-12 students about plant and insect ecology, and train rising students to become future scientists.

name: Topographic controls on transpiration in the East River watershed
description: Transpiration is the upwards flow of water from soil to atmosphere by vegetation. This flux of water is a critical component of the photosynthetic process and an important control on the energy balance of leaves. The spatial and temporal patterns in transpiration have a dominant control of the hydrological balance of watersheds because the use of this water by plants effects how much water delivered by snow or rain remains available downstream for streamflow or groundwater recharge. While transpiration has been an obvious source of interest to ecologists and hydrologists for decades, continuous and distributed measurements of transpiration in alpine systems remain limited. The lack of observed information on transpiration has made it difficult to develop models to predict how and why transpiration varies between species, across hillslopes or in response to climate drivers such as drought. We will use a technique called sap flow to make continuous measurements of transpiration for lodgepole pine, Engelmann spruce, subalpine fir and quaking aspen across topographic gradients in the East River watershed. We will use this data to test how differences in factors such as slope, relief, lithology and upslope drainage influences the water demands between species. We will also test how these abiotic factors interact with biotic factors such as the effective rooting depth and conductivity of xylem tissues to modulate transpiration. We will complement the measurements of transpiration with periodic measurements of the stable isotope ratios of xylem and soil water to help understand the sources of water (such as snow melt vs. summer rain) as well as the soil depth trees are drawing water from. The detailed measurements of transpiration from sap flow will be complemented by a more experimental approach based on continuous measurements of the diameter of trees ? i.e. dendrometry. Changes in the daily cycle of tree circumference is related to storage of water in trees and can therefore be related to total water use. This technique has the advantage of using lower cost and more robust sensors but is less reliable. The work collectively will shed light on how trees compete for available water, particularly at the interface between aspen and conifer stands. This data will be collected synergistically with measurements of canopy temperature from drone flights which can provide spatial information on water use that complements the tree-level temporally continuous data from sap flow. In addition, this data will be used for model validation of a recently developed land surface model. The information gathered on transpiration will also be broadly applicable to understanding the resilience of typical fir, pine, spruce and aspen ecosystems in the western US to climate change.

name: Anoxic microsites control methanogenesis at terrestrial-aquatic interfaces
description:
Anaerobic microsites, a defining feature of soil redox heterogeneity, are zones of oxygen depletion in otherwise oxic environments. Subsequently, anaerobic microsites can serve as hot spots for biogeochemical (BGC) processes, generating and exporting reduced products to oxic environments. Anoxic microsites have been predicted to contribute 21% to the global production of methane (CH4), an important greenhouse gas affecting climate change. They are often generated at terrestrial?aquatic interfaces (TAIs), such as riverine floodplains, which are dynamic transition zones between land and water, where seasonal changes in river and groundwater flow conditions lead to redox fluctuations. As a result, TAIs play a significant role for elemental cycling and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, while only occupying small areas of the Earth?s surface (0.07%?0.22%)._x000D_
Despite the presumed importance of anaerobic microsites in TAIs, significant knowledge gaps still exist regarding their abundance over time and space under varying environmental conditions, as well as their specific contributions to BGC processes, especially with regard to CH4 production._x000D_
Using the novel LOAMS (Laboratory for Observing Anaerobic Microsites in Soils) approach, we will specifically detect and examine the role of anaerobic microsites in methanogenesis and metal redox processes across spatial and temporal scales at current DOE-ESS natural floodplain research sites. The main objectives of this work are to: (i) quantify the abundance and the impact of anaerobic microsites on methanogenesis and elemental speciation; (ii) compare microscale anaerobic microsite characteristics to macroscale field observations of methanogenesis and metal redox chemistry; and (iii) quantify reaction kinetics of relevant BGC processes within anaerobic microsites based on data from controlled laboratory experiments paired with modeling. Furthermore, our experimental data and parametric modeling results will support the future development of refined conceptual and quantitative models, and improve predictions of metal cycling and production of GHG emissions in TAI environments. For this study, we have selected three rivers/creeks (East River, Slate River, Cold Creek) as field sites at the Greater East River Watershed Observatory (GERWO), given that previous field measurements have indicated a potential relevance of anaerobic microsites for methane production at these sites. In addition, these sites allow us to study redox fluctuations due to seasonal changes in hydrological conditions, and provide the possibility to support our research with additional data from the ongoing DOE-BER supported Watershed Function SFA.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Microbiology

name: Plant community dynamics in a changing environment
description: Predicting the responses of species to environmental change is a key goal for community ecology, especially in applied management and restoration contexts. My research focuses on this general challenge in two complementary contexts: alpine plant community assembly, and quaking aspen forest responses to drought and other stressors.

name: Vertebrate antipredator and communication studies
description:
Since 2001, I have had an approved UCLA protocol to study antipredator behavior and communication in free-living birds by employing simple experiments. Many of these projects have been designed to study questions associated with wildlife conservation and management and/or to better understand human impacts on wildlife. In 2008 I extended this UCLA protocol to include other vertebrates (mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and fishes). UCLA supports this (admittedly) very flexible protocol that focuses on methods but not specific questions._x000D_
Much of the proposed work will be conducted by undergraduate students at the RMBL (much of the UCLA work is conducted by students in my field and marine biology classes). Rather than citing specific references to justify a single question, I append relevant publications that illustrate the types of projects we have conducted below. _x000D_
At the RMBL I will design specific projects with the students? interests in mind. Projects will have to fit within procedures identified in this protocol. There are some that might not be focused on 'animals' per se and thus fall outside this protocol. For instance, there may be projects that broadcast sounds in the environment to study the 'habitat acoustics'. Such an experiment would not be targeted towards animals._x000D_
I will provide close supervision of all work. The methods I describe below can be used to ask a variety of research questions and it is these methods that will likely be used by students conducting their projects. The experimental manipulations are relatively noninvasive. The animals are observed, but not handled, and are only minimally stressed or disturbed by a brief change in the environment. Similar sorts of experiments that I've done over the past two decades have caused limited disturbance.

name: The marmots of RMBL
description: The study of yellow-bellied marmots at the RMBL is the third-longest study of free-living, individually-marked mammals in the world. Over the next five years we aim to continue to collect demographic, genetic/genomic, behavioral, and endocrinological data to help develop a comprehensive view of marmot population biology and evolutionary dynamics of a variety of behavioral, physiological and life history traits. We will continue our studies of aging and senescence and hope to expand our studies of the causes and consequences of microbial diversity in the intestinal and oral microbiomes.

name: Drought response as escape from apparent maladaptation
description: The native butterfly Pieris macdunnoughii lays eggs on a non-native, invasive mustard, Thlaspi arvense. The larvae won't eat the plant. This reflects maladaptation on the part of the butterfly to the plant. This maladaptation has persisted for over 150 generations in the Gothic area, in the face of strong selection pressures. We will explore the role of drought in altering plant chemistry, hence larval ability to eat the plant, as a mechanisms that may have allowed the apparent maladaptation to persist in the population.

name: Soulé Butterfly Re-survey
description: This project exploits a butterfly monitoring data set collected by Michael Soulé and his Earthwatch teams from 1982-1991. He collected data on the number of butterflies of specified species seen every 3 days along the Copper Creek trail from RMBL to the first crossing. We propose a re-survey, to examine changes in phenology, abundance and species diversity in the intervening 30-40 years. Additionally, we propose to set up a long-term monitoring program involving RMBL docents to continue this data collection.
researchAreas: Climate change; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology

name: Effect of drought on floral scent and plant-pollinator interactions
description: Plant-pollinator interactions are important for biodiversity and supporting healthy ecosystems. With climate change posing a threat to floral traits that attract pollinators, our focus extends to the often-overlooked olfactory signals and stimuli. Floral scent, composed of diverse volatile organic compounds (VOCs), plays an important role in communication between plants and pollinators. While pollinators use scent to identify and locate rewards, the integration of olfactory stimuli into plant-pollinator networks is still in its early stages. Climate change-induced factors, such as drought and temperature shifts, can disrupt these interactions at both individual and community levels. Our study aims to bridge this knowledge gap, investigating the impact of climate change on floral scent and its role in shaping plant-pollinator networks. By experimentally manipulating precipitation to simulate drought conditions and assessing visual and chemical floral traits across a community, we will employ network analysis to investigate the changes in visitation patterns in plant-pollinator networks under environmental stress. This research aims to advance our understanding of how climate-induced changes in floral scent influence plant-pollinator dynamics at the community level.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Species and functional shifts in plant communities under climate change
description: Scientific understanding of biodiversity responses to climate change have come from ecological modeling; however, the data that go into these models are limited and violate many ecological and statistical assumptions, resulting in unreliable predictions. Therefore, long-term monitoring is the best option for investigating biodiversity shifts due to climate change, especially in areas with reduced human activities that can confound climate effects. This proposed research will revisit and survey plant communities that were surveyed by Dr. Langenheim in 1948-1952 and Dr. Zorio between 2013-2014 to investigate temporal beta diversity and community shifts due to climate change. These sites were selected along elevational gradient giving us a chance to assess plant community resilience and vulnerability under different local conditions.

name: The Spatial Ecology of Environmental Change in the Upper Gunnison Basin
description: This project investigates how rapid climate change is reshaping the mountain landscapes of the Upper Gunnison Basin. By combining advanced technology with traditional fieldwork, the research aims to track these environmental shifts in great detail. Using drones and sensors placed in forest gaps, the team will create 3D maps of temperature and humidity to better understand how trees manage water loss. Additionally, the project will build a sustainable network of weather stations to ensure a reliable, long-term record of local climate and snow conditions, preserving crucial historical data. The team will also continue vital ongoing monitoring efforts. This includes generating "Flower Forecasts" to predict wildflower blooms?verified by community "Flower Blitz" events ?and using aerial imagery paired with tree-ring analysis to monitor forest health. All collected data feeds into the RMBL Spatial Data Platform, a digital atlas that provides detailed environmental maps to scientists and the public, helping us understand the resilience of these fragile high-altitude ecosystems.

name: Effects of herbivory on life-history and long-term demography.
description: The effects of herbivore damage on plant reproductive success are most often assessed by counting fruit and seed production over a few years. Long-term, demographic data sets can be extraordinarily useful in elucidating patterns that cannot be revealed within the timeframe of a typical, 2-4 year project. I have monitored the demography of several populations of two long-lived, perennial plants, Sticky Polemonium (Polemonium foliosissimum) and Scarlet Gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata) in and around the RMBL, off and on, for over 12 years for each species. Both are subject to frequent predispersal seed predation and herbivory by deer which sometimes reduces their annual reproductive success to zero. The two species are uniquely different in that one, Scarlet Gilia, is a long-lived but monocarpic perennial and the other, Sticky Polemonium, also a long-lived perennial, exhibits a rare breeding system (gynodioecy) in which some individuals are typical, hermaphrodites while others function only as females. These differences in reproductive strategies, along with other life-history traits, provide exciting opportunities to ask questions about the effects of herbivory on demographic processes, sex-ratios, and life-history traits. Over the next five years, I aim to accomplish two overarching goals: 1) analyze my long-term data sets for each species to reveal the ways in which herbivore damage affects life history traits and population growth rates; and 2) continue to monitor populations of Sticky Polemonium to examine the stability of sex ratios within and among populations over time and assess if herbivory levels are correlated with changes in sex ratios.
researchAreas: Long-term research; Plant biology; Species Interactions

name: Pollination Network Structure, Function, and Response to Perturbation
description:
This renewal research application covers three distinct but related projects, all focused on pollination networks, their responses to perturbation, and the relationship between their structure and function._x000D_
The first project, ?Quantitative Network Structure and Function? has two primary objectives: A) accurately measuring of quantitative network structure (i.e. intensity of interactions) with a focus on testing predictions about quantitative structure from theoretical work we are leading; and B) comparing network structure and function (seed production across multiple plant species) in drought (2018, 2020, 2021, potential future years) vs. non-drought years (2016, 2017, 2019, potential future years)._x000D_
The second project, ?Snowmelt Acceleration and Pollination Network Structure and Function?, is focused on temporally shuffling interaction partners in pollination networks via medium-scale (10 x 14 m) snowmelt acceleration experiments that are controlled and spatially replicated. The temporal re-shuffling occurs via changes in plant flowering phenology in manipulated patches, whereas we expect the pollinator community to remain relatively unchanged given that the scale of movement of individual pollinators is typically much larger than the spatial scale of our plots._x000D_
The third project, ?Understanding Pollinator Functional Responses and Benefit Accrual Under Perturbation? is focused on improving the integration between models and empirical data in pollination networks. In particular, this work will for the first time empirically estimate the functional forms of 1) multi-species pollinator functional responses, i.e. how pollinator visitation changes with plant density, as well as plant and pollinator species identity; and 2) the numerical response (reproductive benefit accrual) of plants with respect to pollinator visits, i.e. how fecundity changes with pollinator visit frequency change. The benefit accrual component will involve new experiments focused on plant seed set. These empirically validated functional forms will then be incorporated into models, which we will subsequently test by conducting short-term perturbation experiments, in a full modeling-empirical cycle.

name: Isolating chytrid fungi from high alpine soils and aquatic habitats
description: I aim to study and identify chytrid fungi from high-altitude soils and water near melting snow in Colorado during the early summer. These fungi, commonly found in wet environments like soil and water, are known to thrive in extreme conditions, including high-elevation regions such as the Colorado mountains. To carry out this research, I will collect samples near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) and work with them on-site in the lab at RMBL. Using specific techniques, I will isolate and grow the fungi in pure cultures before identifying them through DNA sequencing. The most promising samples will be sent back to my home lab at North Carolina State University for cryopreservation and further analysis. During this multi-year project, I aim to uncover the diversity and abundance of chytrids, including new species, to better understand their evolutionary history and ecological roles in high-alpine ecosystems.

name: Long-term studies of evolutionary rescue in plants
description: Climate change is threatening many populations around the world. A population can avoid extinction by dispersal to more favorable locations, but that is not possible for many plants with limited seed dispersal. An alternative is evolutionary change in which changes in traits increase fitness and result in rescue of an otherwise endangered population. Some populations of a subalpine herb, Scarlet gilia, are threatened by increasingly early spring snowmelt due to climate change, which dries the soil and reduces survival. Long-term field data on this species presents a unique opportunity to examine if evolutionary rescue is likely in a plant population. We are measuring the strength of natural selection on several vegetative traits and floral traits (including flower scent), and our many decades data set allows us to examine how selection depends on the date of spring snowmelt that year. Combined with previous estimates of the heritability of traits (which affects speed of evolution), and the direct responses of traits to date of snowmelt (plasticity), we can test whether evolutionary rescue is likely in this species. Our work capitalizes on the longest data set in the world on natural selection on plant morphology to provide one of the first applications of evolutionary rescue models to natural populations.
researchAreas: Climate change; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Pollination

name: Long-term monitoring of bee-plant interactions
description: Our primary research project is an ongoing long-term (8-year) monitoring of wild pollinator populations, floral resources, plant-pollinator interactions, and local climate. Since 2015, we have extensively monitored the abundance and activity of wild bumble bees and floral resource availability at six permanent study sites within the East River Valley at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). Our long-term research aims to address a series of outstanding questions focused on our fundamental understanding of the population and community ecology of plant-pollinator interactions and mutualism. With ongoing monitoring, our project will generate a more mechanistic and predictive understanding of the demographic responses of wild pollinators in the context of pollinator declines and climate change, as well as how and why species interact in nature.

name: Response of plant and microbial respiration to changing cold season climate
description: Winter is changing in the western US mountains. There is less snowfall, snow is melting earlier in the spring, and the warm summers are becoming longer. These changes in winter and water availability impact forests. Belowground in the forest soil, microorganisms break down organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide (CO2), an important greenhouse gas that is warming Earth. Plant roots produce CO2 also, via their metabolism. Our research seeks to understand how changes in winter snowpack influence the amount of CO2 produced in soils in the East River watershed, near Crested Butte, Colorado. We will quantify the production of CO2 by microorganisms and plant roots across different elevations and seasons. We will work in the two main forest types of the region, evergreen spruce/fir and deciduous aspen, applying unique experimental measurements. We will make use of existing long-term measurements to understand how past changes in snow amount and duration of cover have affected soil CO2. Information gathered from our experimental work and data analyses will be used to improve predictions of soil CO2 produced in the future using models. Our proposed work is motivated by the hypothesis that changing winter snow amounts will impact how microorganisms and roots function separately, and thus understanding these influences is necessary to predict how the ecosystems will respond to future climate.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology

name: Joint fates of genetic variation and demography under changing climates
description: In a changing climate, a central research goal is to understand whether and how wild populations will persist despite rapid shifts in environmental drivers like precipitation and temperature. As such, many researchers aim to monitor population dynamics across space and time to discern how variation in environmental drivers shape population growth, and use this information to project performance and viability under future climate scenarios. Much less is known, however, about the consequences of environmental change for genetic variation within populations. The extent and persistence of genetic variation in wild populations determines their ability to adapt evolutionarily to changing conditions, and also may directly influence population dynamics and persistence. In this project, I will establish long-term study sites to jointly monitor population dynamics, environmental variation, and genetic variation across a range of populations of the ecological model organism Boechera stricta, a perennial wildflower in the mustard family. These complementary datasets will allow me to directly track how population performance and genetic polymorphism change over time in response to variation in climate variables like precipitation and temperature, and to test for effects between population-level genetic variation and population viability.
researchAreas: Genetics; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Other

name: Stomatal trait responses to climate change in the Rocky Mountains
description: The RMBL turf transplant experiment, established in 2017, simulates climate change by moving large, intact blocks of plants and soil along a temperature and elevation gradient. By transplanting to the warmer and drier conditions predicted to occur with future climate change, we can observe how the plant?s stomata respond to novel environments. Although annual monitoring has already documented rapid community responses through shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning, little is known about how stomata respond at the morphological and functional levels. The impact of stomatal traits on plant physiology and productivity points to an unresolved mechanism underlying drought stress responses. Because any change in stomatal behavior is crucial for accurately modeling carbon and water cycling under future climatic conditions, understanding stomatal morphology and its plasticity becomes essential. Additional data will also be beneficial towards collaborations with the TransPlant Network, an international group of researchers conducting similar turf transplant experiments around the world.

name: Effects of stress on colony-level personality in Western Thatch Ants
description: Cooperation is a complex behavior in which individuals act in ways that increase the reproductive success and survival of others, often at a cost to themselves. Cooperation is observed across a variety of species, from ants, to birds, to humans. Animals can have cooperative personality, meaning that individuals display consistency in their cooperative behavior across time and are consistently different from others. Individual personality can be driven by many physiological systems that are affected by early development and environmental stress. In eusocial species, individuals that make up a colony are so tightly connected they are often referred to as a ?superorganism? that display collective cognition and collective behavior. Therefore, in eusocial species, environmental stressors may affect the physiology of the entire colony, leading to distinct personalities at the level of the colony, not the individual. Colony-level personality in eusocial species is not well studied. In this study, we will examine whether environmental stress (bear attacks and nitrogen changes) leads to variation in cooperative colony personality in the Western thatch ant (Formica obscuripes), a eusocial, invertebrate that engages in a mutualistic relationship with honeydew producers. Specifically, thatch ants engage in a defensive mutualistic relationship with honeydew-producing aphids and will aggressively and cooperatively defend aphids from predation in exchange for their sugary excrement. Previous studies have shown that thatch ants that experience stressors are less aggressive when under threat at the nest and when defending their aphids. Previous work has also shown that nitrogen enrichment, can positively affect ants? interactions with aphids, suggesting nitrogen may mediate some of the negative predator effects. This study investigates how nitrogen enrichment affects the defensive mutualistic behaviors of thatch ants and whether predation and nitrogen?s effect on behavior is drives differences in colony-level personality.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Species Interactions

name: How does longterm N deposition impact pollination interactions in Almont?
description: Nitrogen is being deposited from the atmosphere at significant levels at near-global scales, and this deposition has the potential to transform formerly nitrogen limited communities into entirely new spaces, with altered growth, traits, and interactions with other species. In spite of this significance, it is poorly understood how long term nitrogen deposition impacts plant-pollinator interactions, which are of special concern to humanity due to the billions of dollars per year that pollination represents as an ecosystem service. Through collaboration with Josh Grinath (Idaho State University), I plan to utilize his 17 year nitrogen addition experiment at the Almont Triangle (Gunnison County) to assess how plant-pollinator interactions are affected by nitrogen deposition. I will survey interactions between plants and pollinators for one hour per experimental plot per week, and then I will construct interaction networks to compare the network structure throughout the growing season between nitrogen addition plots and control plots using the r package bipartite. Ultimately, this work stands to demonstrate how nitrogen deposition (exacerbated by anthropogenic emissions) impacts plant-pollinator community structure and interactions.

name: Adaptation of bumblebee traplines to natural variation in flower density
description: Bumblebee workers adaptively allocate foraging preferences both across co-occurring flower species in a flower patch and across flower patches in a landscape. These adaptive foraging behaviors improve the resilience of their foraging rates to spatial and temporal variation in resource availability. In my first dissertation chapter I characterized the functional response form of within-patch foraging rates with respect to flower density. In this project, I will characterize the functional response form of across patch foraging rates with respect to flower density. To do so I will measure how the traplines of bumblebee workers evolve during their lifetime, both in terms of patch acceptance rate and patch residence time, in response to natural variation in Delphinium barbeyi density at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). The results of this study will be used to develop a nested functional response model accounting for adaptive foraging behavior of bumblebees both within and across patches. With this model, I will explore the resilience of bumblebee and plant populations to resource perturbations.
researchAreas: Landscape biology; Modeling; Pollination; Theory

name: The effects of tri-trophic interactions on insect population dynamics
description: I will investigate the relative effects of various biotic interactions (e.g., predation, intraguild predation, parasitism) on the introduced population of Gillette?s Checkerspot (Euphydryas gillettii) at Gothic, Colorado. Knowledge of the relative magnitude of biotic drivers, oftentimes regulated by abiotic factors, is necessary to understand how populations persist.
researchAreas: Insect biology; Species Interactions

name: General Observations of Plant-Lichen \& Plant-Herbivore Interactions
description: We will continue to conduct a series of surveys/observations in the US Forest Service's Gunnison District and at RMBL to examine plant-lichen associations in alpine meadows and the long-term dynamics of grasshopper populations. The research focused on plant-lichen associations will examine the variety of ways in which the plant influences lichen establishment and growth and the ways in which the lichen influences plant establishment and growth. Preliminary results indicate that the lichen's presence in xeric alpine meadows may be due to an association with the plant. However, the plant's growth appears to be independent of the lichen's presence. In the near term, we will examine the potential influence of the lichen on various aspects of the plant's life history particularly establishment. The current plan is focused on observational studies and no manipulative experiments are being planned at this time. In the near future, we are considering potential experiments that may include manipulations in the plant-lichen system.
researchAreas: Insect biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

name: Assessing drivers of vegetation functional change
description: We use physiological, experimental, theoretical, and observational methods to try to understand what regulates diversity (phylogenetic and functional) and dynamics of subalpine communities and ecosystems at different scales. In particular, we are interested in understanding how diversity influences ecosystem functioning. We are interested in the relative importance of abiotic (namely, climate) and biotic (species interactions, community assembly, and competition) factors in controlling plant community and ecosystem response to climate change. At the largest scales, we study the flux of carbon dioxide from subalpine meadows along an elevational gradient and its relationship to temperature, water availability, plant functional traits and species identity. We also use remote sensing techniques as well as macro ecological approaches to study large scale processes. At the smallest scale, we are studying the mechanisms of community assembly of subalpine meadows.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions; Theory

name: Community response to climate change using a transplant experiment
description: The RMBL turf transplant experiment, established in 2017, simulates climate change by moving large, intact blocks of plants and soil along a temperature and elevation gradient. By transplanting to the warmer and drier conditions predicted to occur with future climate change, we can observe the responses of the soil microbes and plants to novel environments. Annual monitoring has already documented rapid community responses through changes in community composition and functioning. Extending annual monitoring will further enhance our understanding of the resilience and vulnerability of mountain communities and ecosystems. Additional data will also be beneficial towards collaborations with the TransPlant Network, an international group of researchers conducting similar turf transplant experiments around the world, including the newly established Niwot Ridge turf transplant experiment.
researchAreas: Climate change; Plant biology

name: Genomics of adaptation underlying a transition to herbivory
description: Herbivorous insects are among the most successful?and destructive?organisms on Earth. One third of all animal species are herbivorous insects, and they collectively remove over 20% of plant biomass in both natural and agricultural systems. Yet we know surprisingly little about how herbivory originates: how insects transition from ancestral diets like detritus, microbes, or other insects to feeding on living plants. To illuminate this process, we are comparing the genomes and traits of herbivorous insect species with closely-related non-herbivorous relatives, in order to infer the changes that occur when insects evolve to be herbivorous. In particular, we are focusing on fly species closely related to Drosophila melanogaster, a microbe-feeding fly that is the leading model organism for genetics studies. One of these focal herbivorous species, Scaptomyza nigrita, has been studied for decades at RMBL where it feeds exclusively on wild mustard plants along alpine streams and seeps. I plan to collect S. nigrita flies at RMBL, sequence their genome, and use this genome in a broader analysis with other herbivorous and non-herbivorous fly genomes to help illuminate the genetic changes that allow insects to feed on living plants. While our primary goal is to understand how herbivory evolves, this work also has practical implications. By identifying genes and traits essential for herbivory, we aim to uncover new targets for protecting crops from insect pests. More broadly, by studying how organisms adapt to novel diets, we also hope to shed light on genes that mediate the link between diet and health?which may inform our understanding of the relationship between diet and disease in humans.
researchAreas: Genetics; Insect biology; Species Interactions

name: Long-term research on the ecology of ponds in a changing climate
description: High elevation wetlands harbor unique biodiversity, are important components of Rocky Mountain water systems, and are subject to accelerating rates of environmental change. This application summarizes the next 5 years of long-term research by co-PIs Hamish Greig and Amanda Klemmer on the invertebrates that are critical to the diversity and function of high-elevation wetland ecosystems. In 2023, we collected the 34th year of data on wetland caddisflies at a sentinel RMBL field site, the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve, continuing monitoring initiated by Scott Wissinger in 1989. These long-term data document changes in insect abundances and distributions in response to rapid climate change, including several caddisfly species that have moved upslope from wetlands on the valley floors to ponds at treeline. We plan to explore the consequences of fluctuations in the abundance and distributions of these range-expanding species for salamanders that prey on caddisflies, invertebrate communities, and the ecosystem processes such as carbon and nutrient dynamics that influence water quality. We are also working with collaborators to understand how climate alters feedbacks between predator and prey species in pond food webs, and how this influences the response of invertebrates and salamanders to climate stress. In addition to testing new hypotheses, our research will train undergraduate and graduate students, be used as the basis for multiple community outreach events, and the co-PIS will contribute to the administration and strategic direction of RMBL through committee and Board of Trustees service.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Species Interactions

name: Long-term effects of nitrogen deposition and bears in ecological networks
description: Human activities have doubled the amount of biologically-available nitrogen on Earth, much of which is emitted to the atmosphere and falls to the ground far from its source. This blanket of fertilizer, called ?atmospheric nitrogen deposition, has well-studied ecological effects near sources of nitrogen emissions, but much less is understood about the elevated, yet low-level, deposition that occurs more broadly. In particular, it is unclear how low-level nitrogen fertilization indirectly affects relationships among plants, herbivores and predators, especially across the long timespans over which nitrogen deposition occurs. I propose to study how long-term, low-level nitrogen deposition impacts a community composed of plants, arthropods and black bears. My previous research showed that bears can indirectly benefit plants by eating ants and suppressing positive relationships between ants and herbivorous insects, but that the effects of bears weakened under short-term nitrogen enrichment. Here, I will extend this ongoing experiment to a total of 18 years to evaluate how long-term exposure to low-level nitrogen enrichment affects these relationships. I will also study spatial and temporal variation in bear consumption of ants. This work will aid our understanding of the repercussions of nitrogen pollution and inform the management of both nitrogen deposition and bears.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Atmospheric Science; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions; Vertebrate biology

name: Carbon storage in created freshwater marshes: A 40 year study
description: Wetland soils contain some of the highest stores of soil carbon in the global biosphere. However, there is little understanding of the quantity and distribution of carbon stored in our remaining wetlands which is important to the societal goal of limiting release of carbon to the atmosphere to hinder climate change. Under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, draining of wetlands hydrologically connected by surface waters to a navigable waterway may require wetland mitigation whereby a developer constructs a wetland to offset the loss of the original drained wetland. Previous research by Gutrich, Taylor and Fennessy (2009) has assessed the floristic community development over time of constructed inland freshwater marshes compared to natural reference wetland sites. In this study, we propose to assess the carbon storage and accretion in soils of constructed wetlands in Colorado that now display over 40 years of ecological succession since construction. This scientific research is critical to the management of inland freshwater wetlands in the United States as carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic carbon release to the troposphere.
researchAreas: Climate science; Long-term research

name: Vegetation Recovery after Termination of Heating
description: Much research at RMBL and elsewhere has focused on the effects of climate warming on plant communities. Less studied is how these communities will recover upon termination of heating. Although society is unlikely to actually reduce atmospheric greenhouse gas levels in the coming decades, it is nevertheless of interest to understand how reversible are the ecological effects of warming. Do ecosystems undergo tipping-point-like transitions under warming that lock in change even when warming is reversed, or can we expect recovery of our altered ecosystems should society ever be able to undo the current phase of warming? If so, on what time scale? RMBL provides an opportunity to address these questions by taking advantage of the termination in 2019 of the long-term meadow-warming experiment. In that experiment, measurements revealed significant shifts in plant dominance and flowering success in heated versus control plots. This study will measure these same vegetation variables at least up to 7 years post-termination, to determine the degree to which vegetation in the former heated plots is recovering to levels observed in the former control plots.
researchAreas: Atmospheric Science; Climate change; Community ecology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Theory

name: Lupinus argenteus reproductive ecology
description:
Like color and shape, floral scent helps plants communicate with animals. But attraction via scent is not limited to pollinators, scent can also attract herbivores and, potentially, the natural enemies of these herbivores. Likewise, even while attracting some species, scent can repel others. Thus, floral scent plays many important roles in the ecology and reproductive biology of the plants which produce it. There is enormous variation in floral scent both between and within plant species, and this holds implications for variation in the interactions between individual plants and their environments. However, variation in scent within and among plant species remains poorly understood. _x000D_
Some populations of silvery lupine (Lupinus argenteus) have conspicuously strong scent, while others seem completely scentless. This variation appears to depend on elevation, with populations high in the alpine zone emitting strong scent, and lower montane and sub-alpine populations emitting little if any scent, and populations at intermediate elevations exhibiting a mixture of these traits. In 2017 and 2018 we analyzed lupine scent from one sub-alpine, one alpine, and one intermediate population near RMBL._x000D_
We found that these populations showed strong differences in scent characteristics, and that, in the intermediate population, some individuals produce more alpine- or subalpine-like scent characteristics. _x000D_
We hope to conduct further studies to try to understand which factors are important for generation this variation, what the significance of this variation is for the plants and the animals that they interact with, and whether and how climate change may affect these plant traits and their impact on their communities.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Pollination ecology in Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii
description: This research description proposes two projects for the summer 2026 field season. The first project aim to investigate hummingbird pollination of Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii, with a focus on quantifying the interaction outcomes for both the birds and the plants in these interaction. Specifically, this project will measure the per-visit seed set affected by Broad-tailed and Rufous hummingbirds, as well as the per-visit energy gain hummingbirds receive from consuming floral nectar. Additionally, this project will investigate whether these per-visit measures of interaction benefit are correlated with floral shape, specifically length and width. The second project aims to investigate passive acoustic monitoring as a tool for monitoring pollination visits from different pollinator guilds. Also focused on Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii, this second project will deploy acoustic monitors into the field to collect recordings of pollinator visits. We will then use machine learning to determine the accuracy with which acoustic recordings can be indicative of pollinator guild (e.g., hummingbird, bee, fly).
researchAreas: Pollination; Vertebrate biology

name: Consequences of phenological shifts and pollination for plant populations
description:
Non-technical Abstract (Project 1):_x000D_
Climate change is predicted to decrease biodiversity by increasing the extinction risk of many species, but there are very few examples of climate change actually leading to population declines, because this is a challenging topic to study. One prominent way that climate change is expected to affect populations is by changes in the timing of life-cycle events, such as flowering date or date of emergence from hibernation. Despite changes in the timing of such events being one of the most widespread biological responses to climate change, incredibly little is known about whether and how changes in timing affect popualtions, especially for plants. This project therefore aims to link climate change-induced shifts in the timing of life-cycle events, such as leaf-out and flowering, to plant population dynamics. We are conducting a field experiment where we experimentally advance the timing of leaf-out and flowering in several plant species by melting the snow early. These plants will be compared to control plants to learn how these earlier life-cycle events affect plant survival and reproduction. The data from the field study will be used to build population models that will allow us to understand whether earlier life-cycle events increase or decrease plant popualtions, and why (or have no effect). In doing so, this project will be one of the most comprehensive assessments to date of the risk that climate change-induced earlier life-cycle events pose to plant biodiversity._x000D_
Non-technical Abstract (Project 2):_x000D_
Pollinator populations are declining, but we have a very poor understanding of the ecological consequences of these declines. There is widespread concern that many flowering plant species will decline in tandem with pollinators because approximately 87% of flowering plants rely on animal pollination for their reproduction. Increases in pollination typically increase the number of seeds a plant can make, and because of this, scientists who study pollination often assume that changes in the amount of pollination have direct consequences for the persistence of plant populations. However, the number of seeds a plant makes typically does not limit population growth, especially for perennial plants. This suggests that alterations to pollination may not actually have extensive consequences for plant populations. But no studies have connected pollinator-mediated declines in seed output to the actual ability of a plant population to persist. This project makes that connection using mathematical population models informed by data from a field experiment. In doing so, this project will advance basic scientific knowledge by bridging two ecological subfields that are surprisingly disconnected, and it will increase our understanding of the ecological consequences of pollinator declines.

name: Underwood-Inouye long-term phenology
description: The long-term phenology project tracks the flowering phenology (timing within season) for ~130 plant species in 35 permanent plots in the RMBL area. This dataset shows evidence of climate change advancing the flowering times of most species.

name: Motus station at RMBL
description: I propose to establish a transect, or potentially a small grid, of sensors for detecting radio tags on Broadtailed Hummingbirds or other migratory birds (tagged elsewhere) passing nearby. I would like to confirm an observation from several years ago that male hummingbirds fly about a thousand feet up the side of the valley to roost at night. I will collaborate with graduate student Katja Kochvar on her behavioral study of territorial male Broadtailed Hummingbirds. The sensors would be accessible to any other RMBL researchers who want to put radio tags on animals.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

name: Long-term studies of wildflowers and pollinators
description: I propose to continue studies initiated in 1973 on flowering phenology and plant demography, and hummingbird demography. Also similar studies initiated more recently but mostly decades ago. Phenology will be monitored 3X/week in permanent plots, and individually tagged plants of three species will be monitored annually. Other annual counts include the number of flowering Frasera speciosa in the East River valley. A long-term Malaise trap study in the Research Meadow will be continued, with two different types of traps collecting samples 2-3 days/week. I will continue efforts to reduce deer herbivory in my study plots and to estimate the resident deer population. I will continue establishment of a Motus station for tracking radio-tagged animals, continue collaboration with Cassie Stoddard?s lab members, and initiate a collaboration on songbirds with Savannah Troy.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

name: Bee phenology and abundance, disease, and invasive plants
description: My five-year research plan is split across four projects. (Projects 1 and 2) Assessing how climate variability affects bee phenology and abundance and the mechanisms involved. We will add to a 15-year dataset that is addressing how climate and flowering patterns directly and indirectly affect the phenology and abundance of bees, and how bee life history traits may buffer them (or make them more susceptible) to changes in climate. This dataset is publicly available online and is well-resolved to the species level, making it an exemplary resource for not only my lab and the RMBL community but also the scientific community at large. (Project 3) Effects of sunflower pollen on bee disease. We are building off a tritrophic effects framework to assess how pollen diets have indirect effects on bees by mediating host-parasite interactions. (Project 4) Ecology and management of invasive plants. We will finish a long-term management project on Linaria vulgaris assessing how various management strategies affect L. vulgaris abundance and spread.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Disease ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Epidemiology and evolution across environments in a plant?pathogen system
description: Infectious diseases vary in severity across time and space. This variation makes it difficult to forecast epidemics, so there is a need to describe the underlying factors that contribute to diverse disease outcomes across populations. A growing body of work attests to the role of environmental context in shaping epidemics. At the most basic level, environment can alter host and pathogen physiology and landscape distribution. These changes could cascade to affect host and pathogen evolution by altering selection, leading to different coevolutionary trajectories across environments. However, there are few model systems where ecological measures of disease prevalence and severity across environments can be integrated with genetic data to test hypotheses about how ecological context shapes host evolution. Established in 2018, the Flax Rust Project leverages the powerful system of Lewis flax (Linum lewisii), a supalpine wildflower abundant on the slopes near RMBL, and flax rust (Melampsora lini), its conspicuous fungal pathogen. Populations occur across a steep elevational gradient, allowing the measurement of a wide variety of weather conditions that contribute to the spread of disease. Through long-term observation of disease transmission in study populations, we investigate how hosts balance adaptation to both their abiotic environment and their pathogens. Lewis flax is also a burgeoning model system in genomics, so we can further integrate field measurements of disease with genetic information about our study populations to investigate the role of disease in molecular evolution of this host. Understanding the impacts of environment on epidemics and host evolution will shed light on how disease might be expected to shift as the climate warms and whether we expect hosts to adapt to changing pressures.
researchAreas: Climate change; Disease ecology; Genetics; Landscape biology; Species Interactions

name: Stream Tracker: Documenting flow duration on non-perennial streams
Long-term monitoring of solitary bee populations under climate change
description: Understanding the consequences of climate change for insect pollinators, plants, and their interactions is critical to sustaining ecosystems and the human food supply. While mounting evidence indicates that climate change is affecting bee abundance, studies are still scarce that document the mechanisms underlying these patterns. In particular, few studies have examined the consequences of climate change for bee reproductive output and survival during different life cycle stages. To fill this knowledge gap, this long-term study aims to understand the population dynamics of solitary bee species in the family Megachilidae. These species provide an ideal study system to identify the sensitivity of solitary bee demographic metrics to climate variation.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Integrating resource allocation, vision, and fitness in Speyeria mormonia
description:
Using the Mormon fritillary ( Speyeria mormonia) butterfly as a study system, I will study the adult morphology and reproductive behavior of adults in the field, while also examining how these traits are affected by larval dietary stress in the laboratory. At the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL), I will complete behavior observations, assess visual capabilities of males, determine the fecundity of females, and measure both male and female adult morphology (I.e., wing size, wing color, and body size). Moreover, I will be examining the density of S. mormonia larval host plants ( Viola spp.) each year. These data will be collected every year to determine whether there is an observable change throughout time and whether this change can be explained by other variables. These data collected at RMBL will also be compared to laboratory data at the University of South Carolina in which I will conduct an experiment examining whether larval dietary stress impacts adult behavior and morphology to determine whether these measurements vary from field measurements. _x000D_
 These experiments can allow us to assess the potential impacts of resource deficiencies on adult reproduction and survival. Additionally, comparing data across-years will provide a better understanding of how this system changes across time and whether there are realized, observable effects of larval resource deficiency on adult fitness.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Insect biology

name: Decoupling plant and mycorrhizal fungal phenology in the Anthropocene
description: Plants do not live in isolation. Instead, they associate with multitudes of organisms, including mycorrhizal fungi belowground. These fungi acquire most plant nutrients and water in exchange for sugar. However, interactions between plants and mycorrhizal fungi may be disrupted as the climate changes. This project examines the potential for relationships between plants and mycorrhizal fungi to be disrupted as snowmelt timing shifts with global warming. We will examine the growth and composition of plants and fungi as well as soil nutrient concentrations in slopes and aspects with different snowmelt dates and in a three year long snowmelt manipulation. All data will be fed into an ecosystem model to scale our findings to the global scale.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Microbiomes; Modeling; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions

name: Wildflower Reproduction Phenology and Seed Traits under Early Snowmelt
description: As snow melts earlier in the spring due to climate change, it has the potential to cause shifts in flowering time, especially for spring wildflowers. However, research on this topic often focuses solely on flowering time, with little regard for subsequent seed production and maturation timing. Cohesive research on the entire reproductive stage (flowering and seed production), and how timing of this stage impacts seed traits, is crucial for truly understanding the effects of early snowmelt on wildflower reproduction. Therefore, for three seasons, I will monitor the flowering and seed maturation of six subalpine spring wildflower species at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory from both early snowmelt and control plots. I will then collect a subset of these seeds and analyze their viability, germination, and traits in the Chicago Botanic Garden laboratory and greenhouses.The results of this study will provide novel insight into early snowmelt impacts on spring wildflowers, as well as provide a framework for restorationists who struggle to determine the appropriate seed collection timing and quantity under climate change.
researchAreas: Phenology; Plant biology

name: Exploring the Drivers of Variation in Broad-tailed Hummingbird Displays
description: This project will explore the factors that drive variation in Broad-tailed Hummingbird male courtship display behavior on territories. Detailed characterization of male territories and behavioral observation across the breeding season will allow us to assess the environmental features that drive variation in display effort. Experimental playbacks studies will elucidate the features of female cues that are most salient in eliciting male displays. Together, these studies will give us a better picture of when and why males perform these conspicuous displays.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Phenology

name: Abiotic and biotic controls on chemical weathering rates
description:
Precipitation falling on mountainous watersheds is exposed to surface and subsurface processing, such as chemical weathering, before eventually leaving as streamflow. In turn, this processing is governed by a variety of abiotic and biotic interactions involving, e.g., the type of rock that governs geomorphology and mineralization and the type of vegetation that can generate acidity. The proposed work will focus on the role of vegetation as a means to influence water chemistry and quality. By employing a multi-scale approach, the project will address the following questions: 1) Does landscape-scale heterogeneity in vegetation, climate, and geology impart unique, spatially-variable signatures on soil production and chemical weathering rates? 2) What roles do the legacies of Pleistocene glaciation and Holocene geomorphic processes play in determining modern-day solute concentrations in surface waters? 3) Are physical erosion and chemical weathering rates linked at the watershed scale, and can these rates be predicted from watershed characteristics? These questions will be addressed in the physical and ecological setting of the East River watershed near Crested Butte, Colorado._x000D_
The proposed technical approach will assess controls on weathering and solute generation at the soil profile, landform, and watershed scales. At the soil profile scale, soil production and chemical weathering rates will be quantified with cosmogenic nuclides and geochemical mass balance at sites that span biotic, climatic, and geologic gradients in order to isolate the key drivers of chemical weathering. At the landform scale, solute concentrations in surface waters will be used to assess whether surficial deposits generated by different geomorphic processes impart unique weathering signatures. At the watershed-scale, cosmogenic nuclides will be used to measure erosion rates. A series of reactive transport models will be constructed to place the field-based findings into a framework for making predictions regarding the roles that vegetation, climate, and geomorphology play in solute generation. The proposed research complements ongoing BER investments at the LBNL Watershed Science SFA Science Focus Area.

name: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils
description: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils: Development of an integrated soil functional mapping framework. Soils serve critical roles in most terrestrial ecosystems. In particular, the accumulation of soil organic matter is an important function supporting ecosystem productivity and serving as a feedback to climate change. With the more frequent occurrence of extensive and persistent drought conditions in the Western US, there is an urgent need to improve our ability to map soil organic matter and forecast how it may respond. To address this need, we are developing and testing an integrated framework for measurement, mapping, and modeling of soil functions at a regional scale in the East River and surrounding watersheds. This work will result in development of detailed maps of soil properties, a community accessible archive of soil samples, and an integrated framework for modeling changes in soil functions (not limited to soil organic matter storage) across the region.

name: Sinks or sources: beaver pond fluxes of carbon, nutrients, and insects
description: Beaver dams and their complexes of ponds and riparian wetlands are prominent features of small mountain streams and are widely recognized for their ability to alter hydrology, sedimentation, carbon and nutrient cycling, and aquatic insect communities. Yet, our understanding of whether an individual beaver dam?pond complex functions as a source or sink of carbon, nutrients, and aquatic insects remains highly uncertain. In this study, we examine how the position of beaver dams along a stream channel and the vertical height (head height) of dams influence ponds as a sink or source of downstream fluxes of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and insects. Using paired upstream?downstream measurements of stream discharge, chemistry, insect communities, and greenhouse gas exchanges, together with high-resolution drone imagery that characterizes pond and floodplain elevation, geometry, and vegetation type, we will link landscape position and pond geomorphology to carbon, nutrient, and insect dynamics. This work aims to clarify when and where beaver dam?pond complexes enhance retention versus export of materials in mountain streams. The work will be performed over multiple seasons and years to assess how the dams-ponds operate during wet and dry periods. The research is part of a field course focused on aquatic ecosystems ecology and watershed processes and provides hands-on research training for undergraduate and graduate students in aquatic biogeochemistry, hydrology, and ecosystem ecology. Efforts are focused on the East River, Slate River, Oh-be-joyful Ck, and Ohio Ck drainages of the upper Gunnison River, CO watershed where beaver dams occur.
researchAreas: Aquatic Biology; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Food web biology; Hydrology; Insect biology; Landscape biology

name: Larval mayfly fear responses to predator kairomones at RMBL
description: In aquatic ecosystems, predator-prey interactions are largely mediated by chemical cues. Numerous studies in the East River and its tributaries near Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have investigated antipredator behavior involving multiple predators (McIntosh and Peckarsky 1999), but the cues that may mediate these behaviors themselves have not been identified. Through experiments using mayfly larvae as prey, we hope to further confirm these behaviors but also identify the chemical cues the prey are exposed to. These investigations will be part of a larger study looking to determine if a universal fear cue exists across multiple aquatic ecosystems, including coastal ecosystems up into mountain river systems.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology

name: The Effects of Abiotic and Biotic Factors on Bumblebee Phenology
description: Bumblebee abundance at various life stages is affected by a variety of environmental factors like climate and flowers. However, how these environmental factors affect bumblebee phenology is less well understood. Life stages, called ?castes,? are specific events within the life-cycle of a bumblebee colony. They include queens, which emerge in the early season, female workers, which emerge after queens, and males, which emerge later in the summer. I propose to study the emergence timing of bumblebee castes that are found near RMBL, as they relate to floral abundance and snowmelt timing. I will study caste emergence by contributing to an 11-year long bumblebee monitoring project that includes weekly bumblebee monitoring at six distinct fieldsites, as well as weekly floral censuses of flowers pollinated by bumblebees at each of these sites. Additionally, I will assist in the collection of bumblebee legs for a 5-year genetic study on bumblebee colonies in these same sites to better understand how colony size and abundance may impact bumblebee phenology. I will leverage my past three years of fieldwork experience on these specific projects at RMBL to contribute to these long-term datasets. My results will contribute to our understanding of pollinator phenology, as well as the relationship among sequential life events in bumblebees.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Species Interactions

name: In High Places: A feature documentary about long-term ecological research
description: As the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab (RMBL) prepares for its centennial, the tight-knit community of Gothic, Colorado is approaching the end of an era ? one defined by a cohort of extraordinary scientists who first arrived in the 1970s? and kept coming back. "In High Places" (working title) is a feature documentary that traces the extraordinary, interconnected stories of these scientists, their families, and the creatures they?ve studied in the West Elk Mountains for more than half a century. As their careers draw to a close, what will become of these scientists? work, the singular community they helped create and nurture, and the spectacular mountain ecosystem that first drew them all together?

name: Seasonal Cycles Unravel Mysteries of Missing Mountain Water
description:
Snow provides over 60% of water supplies in the Western United States, and in general, spring snow measurements provide a good prediction of summer streamflow. However, in some years, these streamflow predictions are not accurate, and water managers struggle to efficiently allocate water resources. In many studies, warming temperatures correspond to less observed streamflow per unit precipitation input. However, key elements, including basin heterogeneity, gauge undercatch, groundwater flow, and water storage, are often not represented in models or predictions, and physical hydrologic models diverge widely in their hydrologic sensitivity to warming. We will combine distributed observations and modeling to test the following hypotheses. _x000D_
1)	Fall rainstorms recharge soil moisture and groundwater, increasing subsurface connectivity and the efficiency of winter snowpack to generate streamflow. _x000D_
2)	More uniformly-distributed snow cover leads to greater subsurface water connectivity and more efficient water delivery to the stream. More variable snow cover, either through a greater elevational gradient or increased patchiness, leads to less effective recharge and greater evaporative losses. Only modeling that represents subsurface water transfer from snow-covered to snow-free grid cells will represent these effects._x000D_
3)	Warming temperatures and increased rain relative to snow over recent decades have changed snow distributions in ways that decrease runoff efficiency, increasing the frequency of snow free areas at lower elevations fed by snow at higher elevations, which increases basin total evapotranspiration._x000D_
Our questions require both long timeseries and detailed, distributed observations. We propose to first investigate our hypotheses over the well-instrumented East River (Colorado) and Tuolumne River (California) basins. These long-term observations are augmented with detailed distributed surface flux observations obtained during the 2021-23 multi-agency atmospheric campaigns of SAIL, SPLASH, and SOS in the East River basin. We will use models to establish essential process representations and to directly test hypotheses. We will then test for the essential minimum observations and process representations to expand to larger scales. _x000D_
Our study will directly inform modelers and water managers of the key processes that must be represented to accurately predict runoff originating from seasonal snow in mountain watersheds, leading to improved understanding, prediction, and planning at seasonal and longer timescales.
