name: Ecology of wintering mammals int he Rocky Mountains
description:
Western Colorado University Mammalogy Class_x000D_
Ecology of wintering mammals in the Rocky Mountains_x000D_
The class will involve natural history and winter ecology with focus on mammals and the physics of snow. To explore life histories of mammals we will ?hike? throughout the area looking for mammals and their sign, including scat, tracks, and fur. We hope to snowshoe through parts of the townsite where RMBL staff permits, including along the East River and across the river to the base of Gothic Peak. We will also hike north out of the townsite and do additional mammal tracking and natural history study in the National Forest near the East River bridge crossing. We also plan to dig 12 snow pits on USFS lands and where no existing RMBL research plots are located to measure snow depth and thermal profiles and relate these physical properties to mammal winter ecology. We will fill in the pits upon completion of the experiment._x000D_
I will travel to RMBL on a Friday afternoon in January and spend the weekend with 24 students from Western Colorado University at the RMBL huts. We will gather in one of the huts on Friday night to learn about the foundations of mammal tracks and tracking. The following morning we will snowshoe around the Gothic townsite along an RMBL approved path in single file pattern in search of mammals and mammal tracks. On Saturday afternoon we will trek above the RMBL townsite to USDA FS land and break into 6 small groups with each group digging two snow pits. The snow will be trampled by snowshoes on one pit and left untouched for the control pits. Students will measure the depth of each snow event and measure the temperature within each snow layer. On Saturday night we will gather in one of the huts and students will build thermal profiles and answer questions about the impact of human activities on the subnivean environment used by a number of wintering mammal species. They will also create wildlife skits to demonstrate a variety of winter adaptive strategies employed by high elevation mammals. On Sunday morning, we will snowshoe around the townsite and discuss winter ecology of mammals and observe wildlife and their adaptations for the winter environment. We will depart Gothic around 1 pm on Sunday.
researchAreas: Vertebrate biology

name: Wing loading and wing color tradeoffs in Speyeria mormonia
description: I propose to study the tradeoff between wing coloration and wing loading in adult butterflies. Specifically, I am conducting research on the Mormon fritillary butterfly to deduce allocation relationships across butterfly size and the flight season. Wing pigments are expensive to make and are a part of mate signaling, which makes them an interesting allocation pathway to study. Similarly, wing loading is important for males to search for mates and females to search for oviposition sites. These two measurements are indicative of indirect reproductive allocation, which influence the likelihood of acquiring a mate and overall fitness.
researchAreas: Insect biology

name: Insects on Ligusticum
description: Plants are consumed by a variety of insect herbivores. These herbivores vary in abundance from place to place and over time. The purpose of this project is to monitor the abundance and phenology of insects and other arthropods on the focal plant Ligusticum porteri. The primary herbivore of interests are aphids, which colonize host plant flowering stalks. Since 2017, we have conducted weekly censuses at twenty sites along an elevation gradient. These different sites provide varying combinations of temperature and snow melt timing, which we also monitor. We use these data to assess associations between herbivore abundance and the biotic and abiotic factors that vary among sites and study years. These associations provide insights into the impacts of climate change on plant-herbivore interactions.
researchAreas: Climate change; Insect biology; Phenology; Snow Science

name: Experimental Warming of Ligusticum and Aphids
description: Insects play important roles such as herbivores, pollinators, disease vectors, and decomposers. However, changing patterns of temperature and precipitation are upending the abundances for many insect populations. These population changes may arise from direct effects, as warmer temperatures may accelerate insect population growth. Insects do not exist in isolation, and this project explores the impacts of warming temperatures on the host plants that insects depend on. These plants, in turn, rely on close association with soil microbes, which themselves may be impacted by changing temperatures. Our project will determine the impacts of warming for insect populations arising from this web of above- and belowground interactions.
researchAreas: Climate change; Insect biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

name: The role of ants in plant indirect defense
description: Plants interact with both harmful insects that eat them and helpful insects that protect them. Ants often defend plants from herbivores, but they do so while farming sap-feeding aphids that produce honeydew. This means plants, aphids, and ants form a three-way relationship?one that plants may be able to influence through their own defensive chemistry. This project investigates how activating plant defense hormones affects aphid growth, which ant species arrive, and how much protection those ants ultimately provide. Because ant species differ greatly in how aggressively they defend plants, even small changes in which ants show up can alter plant outcomes. This project tests these ideas in the well-studied aspen?aphid?ant system. This project also asks whether plants can ?anticipate help? from ants. Using young aspen sunflower, the project will examine whether simple exposure to ants?before plants offer rewards?leads them to invest less in costly chemical defenses because they expect protection. Together, these studies will reveal how plants shape ant behavior and how indirect defense fits into broader plant strategies in natural communities.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Theory

name: Investigating the Ecological Significance of Secondary Metabolites in Fruit
description: Plants produce thousands of secondary metabolites ? chemical compounds that mediate ecological interactions ? but the roles of most of these compounds remain unknown, especially outside of leaves. Fruits are particularly rich in secondary metabolites, which shape interactions with seed dispersers, seed predators, and pathogens. However, the ecological effects of fruit secondary metabolites are complex and context-dependent ? the same compound can influence multiple frugivores with opposing effects (e.g., toxins can repel both harmful seed predators and beneficial seed dispersers), and compounds can have synergistic effects. To understand the ecological and evolutionary significance of fruit secondary metabolites, it is therefore essential to determine the combined effects of multiple compounds on a range of frugivores. I propose to investigate how the concentrations and diversity of nutrients and defensive secondary metabolites mediate interactions surrounding fruit. Using observational field and lab studies, experimental manipulations of fruit chemistry, and analytical chemistry techniques, I will assess patterns of secondary metabolite allocation to fruits, as well as how chemical composition and diversity shape seed dispersal and fruit defense. This research will improve understanding of processes critical to plant reproduction and evolution, with potential applications to conservation and agriculture. The data generated will provide the foundation for the PI to establish a longer-term research program at RMBL.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

name: Long term repeat resurveys of the Gothic earthflow plant community
description: Repeat resurveys of a landslide area outside of the Gothic townsite have shown an unusual plant community that has recolonized the site in the past 100 years. This area gives us the opportunity to study plant successional communities in highly disturbed areas, in order to understand their dynamics, productivity, and species diversity. Various biodiversity patterns from macroecological theory can be tested against the data that are collected on this site, to understand how disturbance may affect the plant community structure.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Landscape biology; Theory

name: Authoring disciplinary identities in a community of science practice
description: The purpose of this research is to understand how people learn to do scientific research while participating in research groups and communities of research groups. A community of practice is a "group of people who share a concern or a passion for something they do and learn how to do it better as they interact regularly". A community of science practice (COSP) is a group of people associated with a science discipline(s) who understand and share specialized language, norms, and practices for participation and knowledge generation in the discipline(s). Identity formation as part of a COSP involves learning to legitimately participate in the specialized practices and discourses of the discipline. Such learning is conceptualized as a trajectory of apprenticeship where novices first learn through legitimate forms of peripheral participation, taking on more responsibility and ownership over time as they move towards full participation in the community. COSP research has described full participation as generating new knowledge through research. Structured research experiences are important forms of apprenticeship in a COSP. Although research experiences can have powerful effects on peoples' persistence in science education and research, more research is needed to understand the learning trajectories across different forms of legitimate participation in a COSP, from peripheral to full. This research focuses specifically on how people negotiate and author their science identities through legitimate forms of participation in a COSP.
researchAreas: Other

name: Integrating river science, education, mentoring and community connections
description: RMBL shares the Upper East River basin with other special interests, such as recreation, development of open space associated with the Mt. Crested Butte ski area, abstraction of water for snowmaking and irrigation, hard rock mining and cattle grazing. Such multiple uses of the basin potentially threaten the quality of the receiving streams critical not only to the integrity of the ecosystem, but also to sustaining research, education and community connection functions of RMBL. In 1976 the RMBL obtained a non-consumptive water rights (NCWR) decree that protects minimum flows in streams of the basin. Since that time stream ecologists at RMBL have used invertebrates as biological indicators of stream quality, with the objective of protecting the health and biodiversity of those streams. We have observed some concerning changes over the 50 year time course of this study. For example, changing climate conditions are causing increases in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events, including severe floods, protracted periods of drought and increasing water temperatures, all of which have the potential to degrade the streams of our region. Periodic drought conditions, increasing water temperatures, lower snow pack and earlier spring snowmelt not only affect the distribution and abundance of sensitive species of macroinvertebrates, but also have contributed to proliferation of a nuisance diatom, Didymosphenia geminata (Didymo), which has altered its growth form and has the potential to threaten the health and biodiversity of otherwise pristine tributaries of the Colorado River. The primary goal of this project is to continue ongoing quantitative invertebrate sampling of eight streams in the Upper East River basin two times per summer, estimate biovolume of Didymo, and monitor abiotic parameters, such as water temperatures, light levels, hydrology, and conductivity. This long-term record of biotic and abiotic variables enables early detection of environmental problems and potential effects of climate change. We are positioned to influence public policy to prevent or mitigate human-mediated changes that fall outside the range of acceptable conditions needed to sustain healthy stream biota. We strive to provide a model system for assessing threats to high elevation streams such as human accelerated environmental change, extraction of mineral resources, proliferation of invasive species, population growth and streamflow diversions. This dataset obtained from relatively pristine streams within a backdrop of environmental change can thereby be used as a reference for comparison to streams in other parts of the Colorado River basin that are vulnerable to ongoing and future threats.

name: Beaver wetlands as ecosystem control points for river water quality
description: Beaver dams and the wetlands they create are ubiquitous, landmark features to glaciated river corridors in the West. By building dams and diverting river water into floodplains, beavers fundamentally alter how water flows through a watershed and the biogeochemical processes that occur within the critical zone. Amplified soil weathering conditions, abundant transitional redox boundaries, and heightened aqueous concentrations of iron and dissolved organic matter set the stage for beaver wetlands to be influential bioreactors that can alter downstream water quality. Highly associated with floodplains but marginally understood are colloids; reactive and mobile nanoparticles formed at subsurface redox interfaces, typically rich in iron, organic carbon, and trace metals, and, thus, with the potential to enhance passage of metals and carbon to streams. Unlike hydrologically disconnected floodplains, beaver wetlands are highly engineered systems with substantial advective pathways that allow chemically altered waters, and potentially iron-rich nano-colloids, to be mobilized and transported directly into adjacent streams. My research seeks to understand 1) whether iron-rich colloids are generated in beaver wetlands, 2) whether iron-rich colloids are present in river water downstream of beaver wetlands, 3) how seasonal hydrologic variability influences the abundance and structure of iron within beaver wetlands, and 4) the overall mass loading of iron to rivers from beaver wetlands through surface and subsurface flow paths. Iron particles are widely recognized for their ability to adsorb toxic, redox-sensitive metals from arsenic to uranium, so by focusing on iron this work tracks the water quality implications for harmful trace metals that can be repartitioned within beaver wetlands. In completing this work, I will identify the role beaver wetlands play as an ecosystem control point for river water quality with respect to iron and other affiliated elements and substances.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Hydrology

name: Reconstructing Holocene hydroclimate from sedimentary biomarkers in lakes
description: Alpine regions of the Western US are key sources of freshwater for 10s of millions of people. Modern warming and drying trends in this region threaten the security of this resource, especially in the form of a diminishing snowpack. To better understand the trajectory of water availability in the Rocky Mountains, this project aims to reconstruct (coupled) changes in temperature and hydroclimate over the past ~10,000 years by analyzing lake sediment archives. Using a combination of geophysical and sedimentological analyses, we will reconstruct fluctuations in lake water levels as they respond to prolonged (multi-millennial scale) droughts. We will additionally analyze molecular "fossils" - the organic remains of bacteria and vegetation on the landscape - which can provide information on temperature and precipitation regimes. These data will ultimately be used to better understand the hydrologic history of the region and improve forecasting of its future.

name: Clay formation and organic matter stabilization across an alpine watershed
description:
Soil organic carbon (OC) constitutes the largest terrestrial pool of carbon, and changes in its size have the potential to modulate atmospheric CO2 levels. As such, the underlying controls on OC stabilization and their sensitivities to climatic change have been increasingly scrutinized. The existing paradigm for OC stabilization suggests that due to their high specific surface areas and negatively charged surfaces, secondary clay minerals that form in soil protect OC from oxidation. Thus, a direct relationship between clay mineral abundance and OC may hold across soil types and climates. Despite this understanding, reactive transport models (RTMs) cannot reconcile soil geochemistry and OC profiles, pointing to knowledge gaps regarding organo-mineral interactions and their constitutive controls. Consequently, these challenges result in great uncertainty in the treatment of soil OC dynamics in Earth systems models and their concomitant effects on future climate projections._x000D_
To further understand clay mineral formation and its relationship with OC dynamics over a hydrologic year, Here we propose to advance our understanding of clay mineral formation, OC stabilization, and their_x000D_
controls across a recently deglaciated, headwater catchment (East River watershed) using high-frequency geochemical analyses that track clay mineral formation. Preliminary analyses, including a numerical inversion of a solute time series show that the amount of cation uptake by clay varies on short (event) timescales. These same events also feature changes in dissolved carbon species, which may be plausibly linked to the dynamics of clay mineral cycling. Following these results, we designed preliminary RTMs that include Li isotopes: a novel proxy for clay formation. The models predict a covariation in Li isotope ratios (in sediment and soil water) with solid-phase and dissolved OC. Together, these results support clay mineral formation as a dynamic and seasonally modulated process that is closely linked to OC dynamics. Planned measurements of Li isotope ratios of soil, river water, and bedrock in the East River, along with new RTMs with variable organo-mineral couplings, will help validate these preliminary findings.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Soil/microbial ecology

name: Context-Dependent Life History Responses to Climate Change
description:
Larval salamanders either metamorphose into terrestrial adults (metamorphs) or forego metamorphosis to become gilled, aquatic adults (paedomorphs). Paedomorphs are primarily subject to environmental changes in the aquatic habitat whereas metamorphs are subject to environmental variation affecting both the aquatic and terrestrial environments. Metamorphs and paedomorphs are thus likely to be asymmetrically impacted by climate change. My objectives are to understand how past and future climate variation and climate change impact amphibians using a combination of modeling and field studies. I propose to:_x000D_
A) Compare temperature and water stress impacts of ongoing climate trends under different environmental contexts (in the aquatic and terrestrial environments along an elevational gradient) using data logger-implanted paedomorphs and metamorph salamanders as mobile temperature sensors, salamander biophysical models in different environments. _x000D_
B) Study the thermal physiology of wild aquatic and terrestrial salamanders at different elevations to better understand sources of exposure and resilience to the changing thermal environment they are subjected to under climate change._x000D_
C) Determine the effects of abiotic correlates, e.g., temperature and precipitation, on breeding activity in a wide-ranging frog species.
researchAreas: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

name: Marmot moods: Quantifying affective state in a wild mammal
description: Emotion plays a critical role in shaping animal decision-making and behaviors. However, little is known about the way wild animals experience and express emotion, or affective state, especially over extended periods. In order to predict how species will respond to disturbance, and ultimately adapt in a rapidly changing world, we must understand how to assess their emotional state. The goal of this research is to develop an index that evaluates affective state in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer). Once developed, I will use the index to (1) determine the relationship between affective state and environmental conditions, (2) experimentally validate the index and (3) examine whether emotions influence two fitness metrics. I will use this research to provide a framework that includes taxon-specific measures and can be implemented by other wildlife managers to better understand emotion across wild animal populations. This research will produce a novel study on the mechanisms that underlie wildlife behavior, their long-term consequences for survival and reproduction, and whether human-induced ecological changes may be driving changes in affective state.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

name: Proposed GW/SW interactions course, near on Slate River, July 2026
description: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is holding a training course focusing on field methods for identifying and quantifying stream and groundwater connectivity. For the field components of this class, we intend to focus our stream corridor teaching efforts along the Slate River, along the reach from the Oh Be Joyful campground down to the SLAC research area/Gunsight bridge. Proposed field activities would occur between July 27th and July 31st, 2026. Proposed field components would mainly take place on 7/28 and 7/29 (the rest of the course is offered in a classroom setting), and no equipment would be left installed after the end of the training week. Proposed activities include: The brief installation of seepage meters/piezometers/permeameters, and fiber optic cable (placed at the streambed interface) for collecting distributed temperature measurements; a small drone-based data collection demonstration; non-invasive thermal methods including thermal infrared mapping with cameras and water and bed temperature collection via probes; non-invasive geophysical data collection on the streambanks; and the injection of inert tracers to identify spatially distributed groundwater inflows along the reach via dilution. We plan to make the various field data collected during the course publicly available for possible future research use, and so they could be leveraged to augment the ongoing 'baseflow' related data being collected along the Slate River by the USGS and others. The course teaching will highlight the wide range of RMBL, University, National Laboratory, and Federal data collected throughout the East River watershed related to groundwater-surface water exchange processes.
researchAreas: Hydrology

name: How do the abiotic and biotic environment shape species interactions?
description: Theory predicts the conditions under which species? diets expand or contract. These predictions, such as limited food resources leading to an expanded diet breadth, have experimental support in various systems under controlled conditions. However, we know much less about how these predictions play out under realistic and variable field conditions, nor do we understand their direct and indirect biotic and abiotic drivers. Therefore, I propose to investigate the environmental drivers of interaction specialization and generalization using a long-term (11-yr, ongoing) well-studied plant-pollinator interaction system. Focusing on the floral diets of bumble bees (Bombus spp.), I will analyze how pollinator interaction specialization (i.e. diet breadth) is shaped directly and/or indirectly by biotic factors (e.g., floral abundance), abiotic factors (e.g., climate conditions), and their combinations. This work will leverage 11+ years of data on natural environmental variation and bumble bee floral resource use. While conducting this fieldwork, I will concurrently use my unique training in bumble bee nest searching to locate and document bumble bee nesting traits?the most understudied facet of their life history, and the basis of their population ecology. My results will aid in our fundamental understanding of how ecological interactions are shaped by the environment, and illuminate how plant-pollinator interactions may play out under projected environmental change. I, too, will advance our knowledge of the least understood stage of the bumble bee life cycle through collecting information on bumble bee nesting ecology. Preliminary results from this work have found diet breadth diversity amongst the bumble bee community in our system, with two major groups emerging: relative diet generalists (B. bifarius, B. flavifrons, B. mixtus, B. occidentalis, B. rufocinctus) and diet specialists (B. appositus, B. californicus, B. nevadensis). This information will be used in a structural equation model to untangle how the biotic and abiotic environment has shaped diet diversity in this bumble bee community across the last decade.
researchAreas: Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Microbial Genomics Analysis of the Mt. Emmons Acidic, Metal-Impacted Fen
description: The Mt. Emmons Fen is a unique acidic, naturally metal-impacted wetland system in the Crested Butte area. Sensitive to environmental changes, the Fen provides opportunity to examine how microorganisms, such as the bacteria, can be used as early sentinels of disturbance. Vulnerable to mining impacts, climate change, and hydrological aging, bacterial species and genomic diversities can provide timely information about ecosystem parameters and predict shifts in ecosystem functioning, e.g., carbon sequestration/degradation, elemental cycling, tolerance to metal toxicity. This work continues to build our understanding of the background microbial ecology of the Mt. Emmons Fen in an effort to protect this rare ecosystem.
researchAreas: Microbiology

name: How interactions with mutualists & predators shape plant coexistence
description: Plant community structure is controlled by interactions between individuals that are mediated by shared resources, mutualists, and enemies. It is difficult to study each of these three classes of interactions in parallel due to their great complexity. We propose to isolate the relative effects of each class of interactions by a study of perennial plant coexistence. Perennial plants have life cycles in which competition via resources, pollinators, and seed predators are separated temporally. We will therefore manipulate floral communities of four perennial plant species to parameterize a model which identifies how different forms of interaction impact the viability of plant coexistence and pathways of community assembly.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

name: Patterns of Diversity in Rocky Mountain Alpine Flora
description: The latitudinal gradient hypothesis which posits that biodiversity decreases as latitude increases does not show up in all locations or all taxa. In alpine plant communities many factors may play a role in community assembly including climate and elevation. We hope to explore the main drivers of biodiversity in Rocky mountain alpine flora by analyzing taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic diversity. Our study covers paired sites east and west of the continental divide which are found across a relatively narrow longitudinal band but experience different climate. Using this framework we hope to learn what kinds of climatic or latitudinal factors may play the largest role in formation of these communities.
researchAreas: Community ecology; Genetics; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology

name: How does subsurface connectivity regulate water and carbon processes?
description: This research focuses on the layers of soil and bedrock known as the subsurface, and how its physical structure controls the movement of water and carbon into our rivers. While most of our river water travels through the subsurface before reaching the surface, this area remains difficult to study because it is largely "invisible" to traditional observation. Understanding these underground flow paths is critical because dissolved carbon affects the health of aquatic ecosystems, the cost of drinking water treatment, and the global climate. To bridge this gap, our team will use advanced technologies, including airborne sensors, that map the earth's internal structure from above, as well as high-resolution chemical analysis to fingerprint carbon molecules at the molecular level. By studying the Coal Creek watershed in Colorado, we will integrate these new data into powerful computer models to predict how water and carbon transport will change as temperatures rise and weather patterns become more extreme. Ultimately, the project seeks to reveal how the underground "plumbing" of the earth acts as a gatekeeper for the water quality and environmental health of our planet.
researchAreas: Climate change; Climate science; Geology; Hydrology; Modeling

name: Behavior and Ecology of Burying Beetles
description:
The primary project explores many questions related to the behavior and ecology of the burying beetle (Nicrophorus). Burying beetles are well known for their biparental care, which takes place on a small vertebrate carcass (usually a mouse) that they bury underground. The parents prepare the carcass as well as defend it against intruders, ensuring a food supply for their larvae. Behavioral studies provide insight into the factors that influence reproductive and parental decisions and success, such as individual size and age, carcasses quality, soil temperature, and competition from other carrion-feeding species. Long-term (> 25 years) ecological studies provide insight into the factors that influence the distribution and population dynamics of interacting carrion beetle species, including studies linking rodent populations (determined using live capture-mark-release-recapture techniques) to beetle populations (also marked and released), habitat associations based on microclimate, historical range shifts, and the influence of soil temperature and snowmelt on overwinter survival and emergence patterns. Burying beetles and rodent carcasses are also important components of the decomposer food web- and thus we also study their influence on soil nutrients and plant growth._x000D_
Secondary projects include 1) deployment of motion-activated cameras to detect wildlife behaviors and activity on human trails and at key resources such as mineral licks and sapsucker wells and 2) collection of insects for genetic, identification, and taxonomic purposes.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

name: Long-Term Ground Temperature Data to Study Colias meadii Larval Diapause
description: Ground temperatures, used as a proxy for larval body temperature during diapause, are measured with a dense sensor network in the habitats of Colias meadii butterflies. These data, collected every five minutes and 25-100 feet apart for over six years, create a unique record of microclimates in alpine and montane environments. Research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) has shown that Colias meadii populations above and below treeline exhibit distinct thermal adaptations that affect fitness, and stabilizing selection for these adaptations despite the ability to migrate. However, the effects of the environment on larvae during their long overwintering diapause remain less studied. Other insect studies suggest that extreme cold events, such as exposure to 0°F prior to lower temperatures, can influence larval survival and adult fitness. By collecting microclimate data at biologically relevant time and space scales in C. meadii habitats, we are building a unique record of potential thermal shocks that could impact these larvae. The dense dataset also allows us to refine coarse measurements like snowmelt dates, which affect phenology, and develop models to assess variability in rapidly changing habitats, influenced by factors like wind and cloud cover. This research adds to RMBL?s long-term data sets, expands the region's microclimate understanding, and contributes to the thermal ecology of Colias butterflies, a genus studied at RMBL for over 50 years.
researchAreas: Climate change; Climate science; Insect biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Snow Science

name: Ecology and impacts of non-native mustards in the subalpine zone
description: Plants in the Brassicaceae (mustard) family are of broad interest to biologists. Phytochemical compounds unique to the Brassicaceae (i.e., glucosinolates) include secondary compounds that deter generalists, attract specialist insect herbivores, and deter fungal pathogen attacks. The specific concentrations and combinations of these compounds vary across different mustard taxa and may also change in response to abiotic conditions and through time. In high altitude meadow ecosystems like those around RMBL, native mustard species such as Boechera stricta, Cardaminecordifolia, and others are important hosts to specialist butterfly larvae. However in recent years, several exotic mustards such as Thlaspi arvense, Lepidium latifolium, Capsella species and Barbarea vulgaris, have been rapidly increasing in abundance across sub-alpine meadow and grassland/sage habitats, posing potential novel ecological and evolutionary interactions with native butterflies. In other ecosystems, invasive mustards are also known to disrupt native plant-mycorrhizal interactions and we have recently found this to be the case in the subalpine zone as well. The current project is a renewal of ongoing research on the ecology and impacts of non-native mustards in sub-alpine ecosystems. Over the next few years, my general plan of study is to begin to comprehensively document spatial and temporal variation in the phytochemistry and distributions of native and non-native mustard plants in the sub-alpine ecosystem around RMBL and the surrounding landscape. My specific research objectives are to: document abundance and distribution of invasive mustard species across local environmental/elevation gradients; measure temporal and spatial variation in the phytotoxicty and fitness of focal Brassicaceae species; and develop new experiments to test phytochemical responses to specific abiotic variables. The work will involve training new PhD students and REU students at RMBL and the research will inform our understanding of novel species interactions across spatial gradients now and under future climate scenarios.
researchAreas: Climate change; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Phenology; Plant biology

name: Modeling Drivers of Summer Streamflow Changes at the Micro-catchment Scale
description: Mountainous watersheds, such as the Colorado River Basin, are key sources for a diversity of human needs and are under threat from climate change. The Colorado has seen a precipitous drop in river flows, endangering the water supply of 1 in 10 Americans. This study posits increased summertime evapotranspiration (ET) from rising temperatures is a primary driver of this water loss. Furthermore, subsurface flow will continue to subsidize high ET-areas causing future streamflow declines as temperatures in the Colorado River Basin continues to accelerate. To investigate these theories, an intensive monitoring and data collection campaign will occur on the representative micro-catchment of Snodgrass Mountain outside Crested Butte, CO to quantify and bound ET dynamics. Data collected on Snodgrass will be then used to help inform a high-resolution hydrologic model of the watershed to simulate future ET trends, with important implications for water supply and management.

name: Paleoenvironmental reconstruction in the Gunnison Basin from sediments
description: Lake and fen sediments are rich archives of information about past environments. Near RMBL, these sediments have the potential to reach back 18,000 years to the Last Glacial Maximum. Through the analysis of pollen grains, charcoal fragments, and sediment geochemistry, the goal of this project is to reconstruct past vegetation communities, fire dynamics, and climate in greater RMBL region. Increased understanding of the impacts of past climate changes on ecosystems provides valuable information that will help land managers better prepare for future conditions.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science

name: Bio-logging to reveal the hidden lives of Yellow-bellied marmots
description: The goal of this project is to complement the outstanding long-term data collection on Yellow-bellied marmots at RMBL with bio-logging technologies which will allow for remote and continuous behavioral and physiological tracking. We will densely sample marmots? association patterns and movements throughout the day and year-round. These data will give us novel insight into marmots? subterrain behavior and movement ecology - data that is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to collect via human observations. With these new data in hand, we aim to (1) better understand how an increasingly unpredictable subalpine climate drives marmot social relationships and plasticity, (2) illuminate marmot?s below-ground social lives for the first time and how above- and below-ground behaviors covary, and (3) map wild marmot?s behavior during hibernation and how summer social behavior may drive hibernation survival and success.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Long-term research

name: Pollination and life history of Erythronium grandiflorum
description: (1) On my property at Irwin, I conduct annual experiments to measure the pollination success of an early-flowering lily. (2) In a transplant garden, I annually record flower production and fruiting success in about 230 plants. Two progress reports have been published. When these plants have entered dormancy, I exhume the corms to be weighed and photographed. The data are archived.

name: Unveiling environmental determinants of nectar phenotypes in a selfer
description: The evolutionary transition from outcrossing to self-pollination is known to have consequences for the genetic and morphological traits of flowering plants. However, little is known about how selection has shaped pollinator-reward phenotypes in selfers. By characterizing (1) the genetic and environmental drivers of nectar variation and (2) the ecological and evolutionary consequences of variable nectar traits in Boechera stricta, my research will explore why nectar reward phenotypes persist in this selfing species. During this project, I will phenotype nectar traits in wild populations of B. stricta at RMBL and employ a genome-wide association study under manipulated environmental conditions at the University of Chicago to determine the relative effects of genetic and environmental variation in shaping nectar traits. Furthermore, I will quantify how variation in nectar traits influence insect visitation, and how this may have shaped long-term patterns of genetic variation across the species range. Finally, I will use a common garden experiment to test whether variation in nectar traits influence fitness in natural conditions. Overall, the results will help reveal why selfing species maintain investment in nectar phenotypes, with implications for understanding genetic and environmental controls of gene flow.
researchAreas: Genetics; Insect biology; Plant biology

name: Phenological mismatch between birds and insects in montane meadows
description: An important frontier in climate change ecology is understanding how community interactions may change because of mismatched phenological shifts. Phenological mismatch between insect prey and American migratory bird species may be emerging and is anticipated to have detrimental consequences on bird reproductive success. Moreover, the abundance and biomass of insect prey in the Rocky Mountains have declined over the past 35 years. Climate effects such as snowmelt timing are drivers of change for many taxa, and consequences may vary by elevation. I ask: Do nest provisioning rates by breeding birds change over time with invertebrate phenology during the summer breeding season in montane wet meadow habitats? Does the peak of insect prey demand by birds align with the current peak of insect abundance and biomass? Does bird reproductive success correlate with invertebrate phenology? And do these dynamics change with elevation? I have established a partnership with the Colorado Parks and Wildlife lead avian biologist (Dr. James Gammonley) with whom I will prepare outcomes of this research for use in guiding management of non-game bird species in the state. I am also studying driver behavior in response to different road signage intended to reduce small animal road mortality. I will experimentally test which style of messaging most reduces observed animal road kill events during peak summer tourism season in the back country.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Vertebrate biology

name: Boechera stricta microbiome evolution II
description: The microbes living on and inside plant organs (the microbiome) can greatly impact the health and growth of the host plant. However, despite recent research into the processes and mechanisms behind these relationships, there is still much to learn about how they evolved. This proposal outlines a plan to study the evolution of plant-microbiome interactions using the wild perennial mustard Boechera stricta as a model system. The project will (1) collect longitudinal data on the microbiome composition of plants from wild B. stricta populations along an elevational transect in Gothic Valley over multiple years, (2) isolate bacteria and fungi from roots of the same plants to create a collection of native strains for use in future experiments, and (3) collect soil samples from nearby existing common garden experiments for use as inocula in future experiments. This work will provide preliminary data and resources for future studies and help build a research program focused on the evolution of B. stricta and its microbes in the context of climate change and water stress.

name: Aquatic invertebrates in beaver ponds of different successional stages
description: As beavers continue to expand their ranges and ecologically engineer streams and wetlands within Colorado, beaver ponds of different ages can be found throughout the landscape. Ponds of different ages have varying levels of sediment accumulation and habitat structure, which could impact which aquatic invertebrates inhabit them. This proposed research aims to determine if older beaver ponds house different aquatic invertebrate communities than newer beaver ponds. Ponds of varying ages and successional stages will be sampled in the Trail Creek drainage and the upper East River valley. Using a 1-m D-net sweep, invertebrates will be caught, identified pondside in the field, enumerated, and released back into the pond. Results will provide insight into the relationship between aquatic invertebrates and beaver engineering.
researchAreas: Aquatic Biology; Community ecology; Insect biology

name: Continuing Archival Research of the Environmental History of RMBL
description: This project will continue conducting historical research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL), a high-altitude biological field station located on the Western Slope of the Colorado Rockies. The Lab was built on the site of an old silver mining town, Gothic, which flourished briefly in the early 1880s. In their anthology The Ecology of Place, editors Ian Billick and Mary Price argue that the power of place often motivates ecologists in the field, and that citizens and scientists could work more collaboratively to solve environmental problems if built upon ?a sense of place that sees humans as part of the ecological system, not separate from it.? This project explicitly investigates this more place-based scientific inquiry developing over time, in a place where perennially returning scientists themselves are becoming nearly ?indigenous,? spending entire careers conducting summer field work to understand the dynamics of specific ecosystems or species.
researchAreas: Long-term research; Other

name: Reproductive phenology in golden-mantled ground squirrels
description: Mammals living in high-altitude environments must time their reproduction carefully so that offspring are born when food is available. For hibernating squirrels, food does not become available in the spring until melting snow stimulates growth of green vegetation, hence these squirrels often must emerge from hibernation and mate before the snow melts. However, we don?t know what cues females use to anticipate the time of snow melt, in order to determine the correct time to mate, and we don?t know what the consequences are for females that mate too late or too early. This study proposes to address both questions. The results will not only increase our understanding of how mammals adapt to the strong seasonality of high-altitude environments, but it also may enhance our understanding of the effects of climate change. Scientists fear that one consequence of warming temperatures is that the cues that animals use to anticipate seasonal events may no longer accurately predict those events.
researchAreas: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Genetics; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

name: Ecological Restoration Following Impacts of Invasive Mustards
description: Anthropogenic pressures such as global trade, increased human population, and climate change have led to the introduction of non-native species. As these threats intensify, there is an increasing need for understanding their impacts to native ecosystems and creating new tools restoration post-disturbance. Invasive species in high elevation ecosystems such as subalpine meadows of Colorado are becoming more common. Members of the Brassicaceae (mustards) have recently been introduced into these otherwise pristine areas and are a threat to local diversity and community dynamics. This proposal aims to understand an introduced mustard, Thlaspi arvense, its impacts to the native plant and soil-microbial communities, and to test a new restoration method using microbial inoculation in invaded areas. Over the span of 3 summer field seasons, I will conduct field surveys at Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory to assess T. arvense damage on the diversity and functioning levels of native meadow vegetation and soil communities. A greenhouse experiment will be conducted to test if native microbial inoculation can be used to actively restore diversity and functioning levels post-disturbance. This work has the potential to increase understanding in an area of ecology that is not well understood and provide stakeholders with new, accessible restoration methods.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

name: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
description: My proposed research focuses on how climate change is impacting Tiger Salamander populations through both observation and experimentation. Climate change is particularly strong at high elevations and potentially influential on the biology of amphibians. Building upon three decades of research, my collaborators and I are exploring how changes in temperature and precipitation have and continue to change the life history and population dynamics of this species. Specifically, we propose to continue our population monitoring, increase our environmental monitoring, continue implanting internal temperatures within the salamanders themselves, and conduct a series of experiments aimed at understanding how elevation, temperature, and density may interact to affect important developmental milestones. Additionally, my lab proposes to continue our work at understanding the disease issues affecting Boreal Toads and to explore methods that can aid the restoration of this state-endangered species.

name: Evolutionary Ecology of Floral Color
description: Flower color is central to plant-pollinator interactions, but several outstanding questions remain. How do floral colors vary geographically, i.e. across elevations or between habitats? What are the roles of abiotic agents (e.g. climate) and biotic agents (e.g. pollinators) in shaping floral colors within communities and across gradients? Has climate change shifted the timing or composition of floral colors presented to pollinators? The proposed research will attempt to answer these and other questions by expanding a database of floral spectra from flowering species in the RMBL area. This database can be used to estimate both 'raw' and pollinator-relevant measures of color for each plant species, which in turn can be connected to other RMBL datasets and ongoing experiments (e.g. phenology datasets, vegetation surveys) to answer the specific questions.
researchAreas: Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Expanding Natural History and Community Science Resources at RMBL
description: Natural history collections and community science are increasingly recognized as important data sources for the study of global change biology. Natural history collections, such as herbaria, document changing diversity, distribution, phenology, morphology and genetics over decades and centuries. They also provide many opportunities for education and outreach in taxonomy, ecology and conservation. Community science initiatives, such as iNaturalist, likewise expand the range, in time and space, of data generated on species distributions and phenology and provide an engaging platform for education and outreach in natural history. The natural history collections and curated iNaturalist observations at RMBL serve an increasingly wide array of users and the herbarium is an important resource for plant identification and data archiving for scientists, students and the public. Over the next 5 years I plan to expand and improve the collections, facilitate access to collection data, and utilize natural history collections and community science for research, education and outreach.
researchAreas: Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology

name: Watershed Function Science Focus Area
description: Watersheds provide key resources for human populations, with pressing demands for clean water, food, and energy. In parallel, changing hydroclimate, diminished snowpack, and interacting temperature-driven disturbances, are significantly reshaping interactions within watersheds. The Watershed Function Scientific Focus Area (SFA) is addressing the grand challenges of understanding how mountainous watershed functions respond and adapt to increasing disturbances. Our focus is on understanding the interactions of warming and drought with hydro-biogeochemical functioning in mountainous watersheds of the Upper Colorado River Basin and their retention or release of water, carbon, nitrogen, and other biologically critical elements. Our multi-lab SFA will identify watershed functional traits, which are observable characteristics that mechanistically link to ecosystem performance. These traits will be assessed within a new trait-based hydro-biogeochemical modeling capability (ATS-EcoSIM) that considers watershed compartments? hydrological, ecological, and biogeochemical interactions and adaptation in response to disturbances and feedbacks. High-resolution process-based models will be used to achieve mechanistic understanding across scales. Combining remote sensing, field-based observations, laboratory experiments, and machine learning (ML), we will decipher patterns of watershed functional trait covariance and develop ML-based surrogate models to transfer and scale mechanisms. Our research is organized into three Research Focus Areas (RFAs) and a ModEx integration core, addressing hypotheses related to disturbance impacts and resilience, pathways of adaptation, and trait covariance, aggregation, and transfer. Our goal is to gain a predictive understanding of mountainous watershed function and provide valuable insights for sustainable water resource management, land use planning, and climate change adaptation in mountainous regions worldwide.

name: Geographic variation in floral shape and scent in Polemonium brandegeei
description: We are studying honey Jacob?s ladder (Polemonium brandegeei), a subalpine perennial plant with strongly scented, creamy flowers and skunky leaves. This species is visited by many pollinator groups, including hummingbirds, hawkmoths, and solitary bees. Variation among populations in floral visitors may affect natural selection on floral scent, colour and shape. However, changes in environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, moisture levels) may also cause populations to differ in floral traits. We are comparing flower shape, colour and scent in natural populations ranging from New Mexico to Wyoming to plants from these populations grown in a common greenhouse environment. This study will help our understanding of the relative effects of genetics and environment on floral traits, and potential responses to changes in pollinator abundance.
researchAreas: Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

name: Soil moisture and growth responses to climate extremes in subalpine forests
description: The large objective of this project is to clarify the how environmental and community factors condition subalpine forest responses to climate extremes. Subalpine forests are outsize contributors to the hydrological budget of the Rocky Mountains, but they are exposed to increasing water and temperature stresses associated with climate change. Prior research in these systems has not adequately described the seasonally varying relationships between plant-available water, atmospheric demand, and tree growth. To address these knowledge gaps, I aim to (1) maintain an existing sensor network monitoring soil volumetric water content (?), temperature, conductivity, and atmospheric fluxes to evaluate spatial and temporal variability in soil water dynamics; and (2) to conclude an ongoing dendrochronology campaign seeking to quantify how tree growth rates vary over space and time, across species, and with the instrumented climate record of the watershed. My proposed research is motivated by three core expectations: (1) where water availability is the limiting factor in tree productivity, moisture deficit will be associated with low growth, but there may be other limiting factors present (radiation, pests, or pathogens) that override water limitation; (2) to sustain productivity, trees alternate uptake between shallow and deep water sources where possible and may also redistribute water to replenish dry pools; (3) water availability and plant water use vary across sites as a function of precipitation input, soil properties, and species traits. This effort will shed needed light on the coupling vegetation dynamics and hydrology in headwater forests.
researchAreas: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Snow Science

name: Long-term ecophysiological responses in a montane plant hybrid zone
description: Climate change is causing significant alterations to temperature and precipitation patterns, including more intense and frequent climatic events that can negatively impact species persistence. My overarching goal is to understand whether rapid evolution in response to accelerating climate change can rescue natural populations from extinction, leveraging the unique long-term data set amassed for Ipomopsis wildflowers in the Colorado Rocky Mountains. Over 20 years ago, I determined that the genetic structure of this hybrid zone depends on a mixture of pollinator and habitat-mediated selection; in summer 2026 I will revisit Poverty Gulch, CO to measure the ecophysiological and floral traits that I?ve shown to influence fitness in this system, and determine if these populations have been able to track documented environmental change.
researchAreas: Long-term research; Plant biology

name: The Praxis of Climate Change Researchers
description: Although there are landmark works that study the life worlds of scientists such as "Laboratory Life" by Bruno Latour, little attention has been paid to the ethical foundations that motivate scientists in the field. Using work such as "Because This Land Is Who We Are: Indigenous Practices of Environmental Repossession" as a model, this project intends to interview scientists working at RMBL in an attempt at a philosophical exploration of the virtues, experiences, and ideologies that shape the work happening on the front-line of climate change. Research at RMBL will be paired with similar ethnographies, such as of those involved in the Novel Ecosystem conference, and researchers at the University of Georgia Marine Institute at Sapelo Island.
